context.title: Values and bindings
context.objective: Trace a numeric reassignment and distinguish a value from its type.
context.body:
A value is data, such as the number 3 or the string "Nexus". A binding gives a value a name. Use const when you will not reassign that binding; use let when you will. Assignment with = stores a new value in an existing mutable binding.

const prevents reassigning the binding, not changing the contents of an object. Here we use primitive values only. Quotes make "12" a string, while 12 without quotes is a number. typeof "12" produces the string "string"; typeof 12 produces "number".

Read the example from top to bottom. Both operands of + are numbers, so they are added. After score = score + 2, the new value of score is the number 2. The earlier value is replaced, not added to a separate history. String concatenation and object mutation are outside this introduction.

reply.text: To reassign a binding, ensure you declared it with `let` rather than `const`. When you update a variable like `let count = 5;`, writing `count = count + 1;` replaces the old value (5) with the new result (6). Remember that the assignment operator `=` does not mean equality; it tells the computer to store the result of the right side into the named binding on the left. If you are stuck, check if you are using the correct keyword for a variable that needs to change.

reply.text:
A value is the raw data itself, like the number 5 or the string "Hello". A binding acts as a container that holds that data, allowing you to refer to it by name.

When you use `let`, you create a mutable binding, meaning you can update the value stored inside it later using the assignment operator (`=`). When you assign a new value, the old one is discarded and replaced. 

It is important to distinguish between the value and its type. For example, the number 5 and the string "5" are different types of data. You can check the type of any value using the `typeof` operator, which will return "number" for 5 and "string" for "5". Use `const` if you do not intend to change the binding, and `let` if you need to reassign it.

context.title: Decisions with conditions
context.objective: Trace an if/else branch and distinguish strict equality from assignment.
context.body:
A comparison produces a boolean: true or false. The >= operator means greater than or equal to. An if statement executes its block when its condition is truthy; otherwise its else block executes. In this lesson all conditions are explicit boolean comparisons.

Use === to test strict equality. If the operands have different types, the result is false: 3 === "3" is false because a number and a string are different types. Assignment uses =; it does not test equality.

Trace the comparison before choosing a branch. With minutes = 20, the example prints Practice. With minutes = 10, the comparison 10 >= 15 is false, so only Review is printed. This introduction does not cover every truthy/falsy value or every numeric equality edge case.

reply.text:
An `if` statement allows your code to make decisions. It evaluates a condition, which results in either `true` or `false`. If the condition is `true`, the code inside the `if` block runs. If it is `false`, the code inside the `else` block runs instead.

When comparing values, use `===` for strict equality to ensure both the value and the data type match. Be careful not to confuse this with `=`, which is used for assignment (giving a variable a value). 

For example, if you have `let score = 50;`, the condition `score === 50` is `true`, while `score = 100` would simply change the value of `score` to 100. Always trace your comparisons step-by-step to see which branch your program will take.

context.title: Functions and return values
context.objective: Follow arguments into a function and distinguish returning a value from logging it.
context.body:
A function packages reusable work. A parameter names an input inside the function. An argument is the value supplied when calling it. Each call to addFive gives minutes the supplied argument.

return sends a value back to the caller and ends that function call. console.log displays a value; it does not make an enclosing function return that value. An ordinary function that reaches its end without returning a value returns undefined, not null.

In the example, addFive(10) returns 15, which is stored in planned. A function containing only console.log("Ready") displays Ready but its caller receives undefined. These examples are read-only. Submitted JavaScript is never executed. Async functions and generators are outside this introduction.

rubric: Technically correct and grounded in the supplied lesson; no invented facts, sources or URLs.
Does not choose an exercise option, claim to have assessed the learner, request personal data or award mastery.
Brief and useful for a beginner; plain text, at most 180 words.
Distinguish parameter from argument and return from logging. An ordinary function with no return yields undefined, not null.
Hint must guide substitution/return tracing without answering that addFive(20) returns 25.

reply.text:
To help you distinguish between logging and returning, consider what happens to the data after the function finishes. 

If you use `console.log()`, the value is printed to the console for you to see, but the function itself does not provide a result back to the code that called it. If you try to store the result of that function in a variable, that variable will be `undefined`.

If you use `return`, the function sends a specific value back to the caller. This allows you to capture that value in a variable or use it in further calculations. 

Think of `console.log` as a way to "show your work" on the screen, while `return` is how the function "hands over" the final result to be used elsewhere. Check your code: are you using `return` to pass the value back, or are you just printing it to the console?

reply.text:
A function is a reusable block of code. You define a parameter as a placeholder for input, and when you call the function, you provide an argument—the actual value used for that specific task.

The `return` keyword is how a function sends a result back to the code that called it. Once `return` is executed, the function stops immediately. 

It is important to distinguish `return` from `console.log`. While `console.log` prints information to the console for you to see, it does not provide a value back to your program. If a function finishes its work without a `return` statement, it automatically returns `undefined`. 

Think of `return` as handing a finished product back to the caller, whereas `console.log` is simply showing the product to someone watching.
